title: Integer factorization records
section: Records for efforts by quantum computers
text:
The largest number reliably factored by Shor's algorithm, rather than some other quantum method, is 21 which was factored in 2012.[1,2] The number 15 had previously been factored by several labs and subsequent attempts to factorise 35 failed.[2]

Other methods have been used to factorise specific numbers on quantum computers. In April 2012, the factorization of 143 = 13 × 11 by a room-temperature (300 K) NMR adiabatic quantum computer was reported by a group.[3] In November 2014 it was discovered that the factorisation of other numbers could lead to the same equations that were solved in the 2012 paper, thus the 2012 experiment could be considered to have also factored much larger numbers without knowing it.[4,5] In April 2016 the 18-bit number 200,099 was factored using quantum annealing on a D-Wave 2X quantum processor.[6] Shortly after, the number 291,311 was factored using NMR at higher than room temperature.[7] In late 2019, Zapata computing claimed to have factored 1,099,551,473,989,[8] and in 2021 released a paper describing this computation.[9] In 2024, a new approach to embed prime factoring problems into quantum annealers has been proposed, leading to (i) the embedding of 21×12 prime factoring problems into a D-Wave Pegasus architecture; (ii) the factoring of 8,219,999 by using a quantum annealer without exploiting hybrid techniques.[10]

As such, claims of factoring with quantum computers have however been criticized for depending heavily on classical computation to reduce the number of qubits required.[11,12]

For example, the factorization of 1,099,551,473,989 relied on classical pre-processing to reduce the problem to a three-qubit quantum circuit.[9] Furthermore, the three numbers factored in this paper (200,099, 291,311, and 1,099,551,473,989) can easily be factored using Fermat's factorization method, requiring only 3, 1, and 1 iterations of the loop respectively. In 2025, existing factorisation records using a quantum computer were replicated using a VIC-20, highlighting the ease of factoring numbers with particular structures.[2]
